reasons: The excerpt’s test table specifies a platform-native lift study in which Meta or Google randomly assigns users to exposed and holdout groups and measures the conversion difference.
Its stated measure is true incremental conversions from the ad platform, matching the candidate trigger.
The excerpt explicitly defines a DIY geo-holdout as pausing ads in matched test regions and comparing them with control regions.
It identifies the measure as channel-level incrementality across all markets, consistent with the candidate trigger.
The source table defines an on/off experiment as turning a channel or campaign on and off in alternating periods.
The table says this measures the overall revenue impact of the channel, matching the candidate.
The source defines difference-in-differences as comparing outcome changes over time between treatment and control groups.

It says to use it when user-level randomization is not possible but there is a comparable control group, and its method-selection table lists pre/post data for treatment and control as the data requirement.
The excerpt describes CUPED as using pre-experiment data to reduce noise and variance in experiment results.
It recommends CUPED for A/B tests with pre-experiment user data, and the selection table specifies user-level pre-period data.
The source defines switchback testing as randomizing entire environments, including regions or time periods, rather than individual users.
It identifies marketplace experiments with user-level interference, such as search-ranking changes or ad-spend allocation, as the use case and lists time-based randomization as the data requirement.
The excerpt says synthetic control combines imperfect control candidates with weights to create a composite control group that matches the test group as closely as possible.
It recommends the method when no true control group is available and lists panel data across markets as the data requirement.
The source describes BSTS as combining Kalman filtering, spike-and-slab regression, and Bayesian model averaging.
It recommends BSTS for time-series data with strong seasonality when estimating intervention impact without a clean control group, and lists time-series data as required.
The source defines PSM as matching treated customers to control customers with similar treatment propensity based on observed covariates.
It recommends PSM when randomization is unavailable but rich customer data can create comparable groups, with rich customer covariates listed as the data requirement.
The excerpt defines IV as using a variable correlated with treatment but not directly with the outcome except through treatment.
It identifies selection bias or nonrandom treatment assignment, together with a valid instrument, as the applicable condition and data requirement.
The source says RDD exploits a cutoff or threshold at which treatment changes discontinuously.
It recommends RDD for threshold-assigned treatments and lists an assignment variable with a cutoff as the data requirement.
The causal-measurement framework explicitly makes deciding the question to answer its first step.
The framework explicitly makes matching the method to data infrastructure and traffic its second step.

The claim accurately preserves the excerpt’s qualified traffic guidance: stores above 100k monthly visitors can run specified designs, while lower-traffic stores may need BSTS, synthetic control, or longer holdouts.
The dependency on deciding the question first follows the source’s ordered Step 1 then Step 2 framework.
This principle is stated verbatim in the excerpt’s key takeaways.
The following sentence clarifies the distinction: an A/B test identifies which variant won, while a holdout addresses whether the change created otherwise-unavailable value.

The conclusion in the excerpt explicitly says Meta drove measurable incremental value and that the 10%+ conversion lift showed it was not merely taking credit for conversions that would have happened anyway.
The preceding study description supports calling the example a Meta geo-holdout: all Meta campaigns were paused in 10 holdout DMAs.

omissions.description: The framework’s third step directs teams to document each causal analysis, including the question, method, result and confidence interval, and resulting business decision, to build a causal knowledge base.
omissions.quote:
Every holdout, incrementality test, and causal analysis should be documented with:

- The question asked

- The method used

- The result and confidence interval

- The business decision made
